strengths: Addresses a meaningful limitation of GRPO: all-failure rollout groups provide no reward-based learning signal. Hierarchical prompt hints offer a practical way to obtain useful training trajectories.

Reports consistent improvements across five model backbones and seven mathematics benchmarks. For Qwen2.5-Math-7B, average greedy accuracy improves from 45.2% to 50.9%; the avg@16 evaluation also supports an improvement, from 44.8% to 48.1%.

Provides substantial ablations covering hint hierarchy, incremental disclosure, exemption duration, data filtering, and teacher quality. Additional DAPO comparisons and DeepScaleR continuation experiments broaden the empirical evidence.
Includes useful implementation details, pseudocode, prompt templates, hardware specifications, and hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The central optimization claims are overstated. Equations (2)–(4) normalize rewards jointly across different conditioning contexts and retain a hinted trajectory specifically because it succeeded. Matching the numerator and denominator contexts makes the token likelihood ratio sensible, but does not establish preservation of the original GRPO objective or absence of selection bias. Appendix F largely repeats the assertion rather than deriving the objective induced by this sampling procedure.

Reported evaluation details contain consequential inconsistencies. Table 7 specifies 25 AMC problems, yet the main results repeatedly use 2.5-percentage-point increments, incompatible with single-attempt accuracy on 25 problems. Likewise, AIME scores such as 7.2% in Table 1 and 43.1% in Table 17 cannot arise from the stated greedy evaluation on 30 problems. Exact benchmark versions, denominators, and any averaging procedures need clarification.

Statistical and model-selection controls are insufficient. There are no reported independent training seeds or confidence intervals, and the validation split used to select the best checkpoint is unspecified. The headline AIME24 improvement represents four additional correct answers out of 30. Avg@16 helps assess sampling performance but does not resolve training variance or checkpoint-selection bias. Training/evaluation overlap checks are also not documented despite overlapping dataset sources.

Comparisons do not adequately isolate the proposed contribution. Closely related hierarchical guidance methods such as StepHint are discussed but not evaluated. LUFFY mixes expert trajectories rather than simply implementing the prefix-continuation mechanism repeatedly attributed to it. Matched comparisons using identical teacher information, rollout budgets, and prefix-versus-prompt placement would better establish the novelty and advantage of scaffolding.

The efficiency evidence is incomplete. Hint search can require up to 12 additional generations per triggered query, but the paper reports neither total generated tokens nor average search depth. The 12-versus-13-hour comparison measures time to each method's own best checkpoint and excludes offline teacher generation and filtering costs. It therefore does not establish the claimed overall computational advantage.

The proposed mechanism is not convincingly demonstrated. Section 3.2 describes algorithmic plateau detection and persistent per-problem failure, whereas Algorithm 1 uses a fixed exemption threshold and the current all-failure group. Figure 2 does not clarify whether zero-reward counts are measured before hint replacement; post-replacement counts would mechanically favor the method. Graduation counts use different definitions across methods and do not establish durable skill acquisition rather than success on repeatedly trained examples.

Minimal guidance and preserved exploration remain stronger claims than the evidence supports. One sampled completion per hint level cannot identify the genuinely minimal sufficient hint, and the solution-hint template can reveal the final answer. The paper lacks measurements of answer disclosure, reasoning diversity, or transfer on controlled held-out problem families that would distinguish the proposed explanation from ordinary teacher-assisted learning.

strengths: Addresses a relevant limitation of GRPO: all-failure rollout groups provide no reward-based policy gradient. Hierarchical prompt hints offer a practical intervention with relatively simple implementation.

Reports consistent improvements across five model backbones and seven mathematics benchmarks. Qwen2.5-Math-7B improves from 45.2% to 50.9% average accuracy; the supplementary avg@16 evaluation also supports gains beyond the headline greedy-decoding result.
Provides substantial ablations covering hint categories, incremental guidance, exemption duration, data filtering, and teacher choice, alongside additional DAPO and DeepScaleR experiments.
Includes useful implementation details, prompt templates, pseudocode, and hardware specifications.
weaknesses: The central claim of preserving the GRPO objective without introducing bias is not established. Equations (2)–(4) normalize rewards jointly across different conditioning contexts and retain a hinted trajectory specifically because it succeeds. Matching numerator and denominator prompts does not correct this outcome-dependent selection or establish equivalence to the original expected-return objective. Appendix F largely restates the construction rather than justifying these claims.

Novelty and comparative positioning remain insufficiently demonstrated. Closely related hierarchical guidance methods, including the cited StepHint and BREAD, are not evaluated. LUFFY is repeatedly characterized as a prefix-continuation method even though the paper itself describes its mixing of complete expert trajectories. Its comparison therefore does not establish superiority over the broader prefix-guidance paradigm.

The experiments do not adequately separate the proposed mechanism from additional supervision and sampling. Scaf-GRPO uses teacher-generated hints derived from ground-truth solutions and can make up to 12 extra generation attempts per failed group. Missing controls include compute-matched unguided resampling and simpler training on successful hinted trajectories. The reported time to best checkpoint is useful but excludes documented accounting for teacher preprocessing and total generated tokens.

Statistical reliability and model selection are unclear. No independent training seeds or confidence intervals are reported, and the validation dataset and criterion used to select the best checkpoint are unspecified. The headline AIME24 improvement corresponds to four additional correct answers out of 30. Avg@16 strengthens the evidence but does not address training variance or potential checkpoint-selection bias.

Claims about diagnosing genuine capability gaps and internalizing general reasoning exceed the evidence. Algorithm 1 uses a fixed exemption threshold followed by a single all-failure group, rather than the claimed algorithmic detection of persistent stagnation. One stochastic attempt per hint cannot establish minimal necessary guidance. Training-problem graduation counts and an illustrative example also do not distinguish transferable skill acquisition from memorization.

Evaluation documentation contains consequential gaps and inconsistencies. Table 7 lists 25 AMC problems, whereas reported greedy accuracies such as 42.5% and 62.5% cannot arise from that denominator. Training data include AIME, AMC, and MATH sources, but no explicit train–test overlap audit is described. These issues, together with the unresolved methodological claims, prevent the otherwise promising empirical results from meeting the acceptance threshold.

strengths: Addresses a practical limitation of GRPO: all-failure rollout groups provide no reward-based learning signal. Selective, progressively detailed hints offer an intuitive and implementable intervention.

Reports consistent improvements across five model backbones and seven mathematics benchmarks. Qwen2.5-Math-7B improves from 45.2% to 50.9% average accuracy, with gains also persisting under avg@16 evaluation.

Provides substantial ablations covering hint categories, incremental disclosure, the exemption period, data filtering, and teacher quality. Additional DAPO comparisons and continued training of DeepScaleR strengthen the empirical coverage.
Includes useful implementation details, hint-generation prompts, pseudocode, and hardware specifications. The GPQA results provide some evidence of transfer beyond mathematics.
weaknesses: The central optimization claims are overstated. Equations (2)–(4) normalize rewards jointly across different conditioning contexts and retain only successful hinted trajectories after an adaptive search. Matching the numerator and denominator prompts avoids one likelihood-ratio mismatch, but does not establish preservation of the original GRPO objective or absence of selection bias. Appendix F.4's claim of no harmful bias is unsupported; the method needs an explicit characterization as a modified training objective.

Evaluation reporting contains material inconsistencies. Table 7 specifies 25 AMC problems, but reported greedy accuracies such as 42.5% and 62.5% cannot arise from one binary outcome per problem on that set. Likewise, 7.2% on 30 AIME24 problems is incompatible with the stated single-run greedy protocol. The actual benchmark subsets, aggregation procedures, and distinction between reproduced and inherited results need clarification.

The paper reports best-performing checkpoints without specifying an independent checkpoint-selection set or selection rule. Training-seed variability and confidence intervals are absent. The headline AIME24 improvement represents four additional solved problems out of 30; avg@16 supports the direction of improvement but does not resolve training variability or checkpoint-selection concerns.

Comparisons do not sufficiently isolate the proposed contribution. Closely related hierarchical guidance methods such as StepHint and BREAD are discussed but not evaluated. Missing controls include compute-matched unguided resampling, ordinary training on hint-augmented prompts, and matched teacher-supervision baselines. These would distinguish the hierarchy and mixed-group update from extra attempts and additional solution information.

Claims about diagnosing persistent learning stagnation and internalizing reasoning exceed the evidence. Algorithm 1 uses a fixed exemption threshold and a single all-failure group, rather than the described plateau detector or persistent per-problem failure tracking. The first successful stochastic hint attempt is not necessarily minimal guidance. Figure 2 should distinguish pre-intervention unassisted failures from post-replacement failures, and graduation counts on training examples do not by themselves demonstrate transferable skill acquisition.

The efficiency evidence is incomplete: time to each method's separately selected best checkpoint does not account explicitly for offline teacher generation or quantify the additional search rollouts. Together with the unresolved optimization and evaluation issues, this prevents the otherwise promising empirical results from establishing a sufficiently convincing contribution for acceptance.
